# **Serious Game Project: MVP Design Document** {#serious-game-project:-mvp-design-document}

You've identified your topic, tested three different game perspectives, and playtested with real players. Now you're going to document your game in detail before you build it digitally. This design document is your blueprint. It shows what your game looks like, how it works, and why each part matters.

Your design document should have:

* A clear description of your chosen paper prototype
* Sketches and descriptions of your game screens and mechanics
* Justification for why this design serves your learning goal

---

## **Part 2 \- Choose Your Paper Prototype**

**Choose (and refine) your best paper prototype. Add pictures of it here:**

| ![][image1]![][image2]![][image3]   Miles and Knox drew it  |
| :---- |

**Describe how to play your paper prototype.**

| To play out our paper prototype, you're a teenage character living in poverty. You'll play out his day and must go through each challenge he faces. You will encounter different people throughout the day, some interactions will be positive, but most will be negative. Each time you encounter a person to talk with them, you will only be restricted to using multiple choice options, and each choice you make leads to a different outcome.  To prevent the player from just choosing the aggressive/safe option all the time, we added a new mechanic called a patience bar. A safe option lowers your patience, and a bad option raises it. When your patience bar runs out, you are only restricted to the worst option. For example, the images show the teen walking to school, and when he gets to school, the teacher reprimands him for being late on his homework, and then he has three options, one, apologize to the teacher, two, ignore him, or three, curse the teacher out. And these options, in turn, lead to more options. For example, if the player chooses to curse out his teacher, he then gets sent to the principal's office and faces potential suspension. Or if he ignores his teacher, he then gets a zero on the assignment and fails the class. Later on in the day, he stops at the gas station after work, and he gets the option to chill with the people hanging out outside. Our character likes these guys, but his mom hates them because they have no future and they are in trouble. If he hangs out with them, his mom will yell at him very badly and maybe kick him out of the house, but he also does not have that many friends at school, and these guys accept him more than others. Our character feels as if these are his real friends, even if they are not. On the other hand, he could just go home and not hang out with them. This will make his mom happy, but our character will be bored and won't get to talk to his friends. This will reduce his patience level, which will make him have to choose worse options in the future. Such as with his teacher or his homework.  |
| :---- |

**What made this prototype work?** Describe one moment from playtesting that showed you this was the right direction. What did a playtester do or say?

| The playtesters said that this is much clearer than our prototype, and they said that it makes sense, but we need to fix our storytelling.  |
| :---- |

## **Part 3 \- Mechanics, Dynamics, Aesthetics**

These three things work together to create your game experience.

**What is your most important mechanic?** The rule or action. (Example: "The player chooses which person to help with a limited time per turn.")

| Our most important mechanic is by far our multiple-choice option. This mechanic led to different outcomes. It created a dynamic loop of curiosity because you'll never know what comes next. It makes the player feel in control of their character's actions and decisions, and it gives a more personal feel. That's why it's the most important mechanic.   |
| :---- |

**What dynamic should this elicit?** What happens as a result? What tension or situation does the mechanic create? (Example: "The player faces real tension because they can't help everyone.")

| In a game about poverty, the multiple-choice mechanics create a dynamic where the player feels the weight of their actions and limitations, every choice has a cost, which forces the player to prioritize survival over fun. Another dynamic loop of curiosity. This mechanic creates a situation where the player is constantly  |
| :---- |

**What aesthetic should players feel?** What do you want it to feel like to play? (Example: "Stress. Moral weight. The feeling of helplessness in the face of competing needs.")

|  |
| :---- |
| The players should feel stressed and pressured during the game. Every choice they make should feel hard and have no perfect answer. It should also feel frustrating because things don’t always work out. The Players should feel overwhelmed and tired so they understand how hard poverty is. |

**How do these three work together to serve your learning goal?**

| Our mechanics, dynamics, and aesthetics work together in multiple ways to help our players understand poverty. Firstly, our mechanics show the hopelessness that many people in poverty feel, where every mistake they make is punished far worse. And this is done through our patience system, where they physically can't choose the good option every time. This, in turn, leads to the dynamic of having to strategically choose how many good options and bad options they choose. And lastly, our aesthetics try to mimic the feeling of misery that abject poverty creates. We want the player to feel like they have no options and that just the surroundings around them are bleak.  |
| :---- |

## **Part 4 \- Mechanics and Story Alignment**

Now let’s flesh out your paper prototype into a game idea\! In a serious game, your mechanics should embody your message, not just decorate it.

**What story are you telling?** Briefly describe the scenario, the world, or the situation the player enters.

| The player enters what a daily life would be for a teen that experiences poverty, and they will go through the day and be faced with the different challenges as in irl.   |
| :---- |

**How do your mechanics embody this story?** Don't explain it through dialogue or cutscenes. Explain it through what the player actually does. Why does that specific action matter thematically?

| Our mechanics embody the story by forcing players to make difficult trade-offs through multiple-choice questions, such as choosing between an aggressive option and a peaceful option. This creates a scenario of stress and a feeling of responsibility where the player experiences how easily a single fun or aggressive choice can lead to a massive spiral of consequences. The overall goal is for everyone to understand how different life can be for other people, and hopefully, this game will help them better understand the different living situations of the people. Hopefully, they will learn to respect them just as well as they do their own friends.  |
| :---- |

---

## **Part 5 \- Goals, Subgoals, and Pacing**

**Overall goal:** What is the player trying to accomplish? This should connect to your learning goal.

| For the user to walk away understanding poverty and how they can change their perspective to help this growing problem.  |
| :---- |

**Subgoals:** What are 2-4 smaller objectives the player works toward on the way to the overall goal? (List them in order.)

| Some smaller objectives are to maintain stability, be patient, avoid rushing, be smart, and consider the immediate consequences of your actions.  |
| :---- |

**Pacing:** How does the game get harder or more complex? When does the player feel successful? When do they feel challenged? You can sketch a quick graph, describe it, or both.

| The game gets harder because of the patience mechanic. Eventually, you'll just have to choose the bad options, which will lead to worse ones. This is supposed to challenge the player a lot and make it so that they do not just choose the “good option” every time, and make the game much harder. There are a couple of good endings and bad endings, which are meant to make the character feel successful and challenged.   |
| :---- |
